writeup.1: Left of Field Golf is four years old and runs out of Sydney. Nick Ilias started it in 2022 in his brother’s old bedroom, which he described in a journal entry written in Paris three years later as “a small room filled with everything from late-night brainstorming sessions to boxes stacked high with stock.”
writeup.2: Ilias started from a complaint a lot of players will recognise. “When I first started playing the game, getting dressed for golf felt like a lose-lose situation. The outfits I wanted to wear made me feel out of place in the pro shop. Adhering to the dress code just didn’t feel natural, either.”
writeup.3: What he built is not, as it is often described, a brand about Australian landscapes. It is a brand about silhouette. The aim in their own words is clothing “inspired by the attitude and silhouettes of surf and skate apparel, with design touches golfers can appreciate as their own,” and then, flatly: “Our mission isn’t to create products that scream ‘golf’.” That is why the shorts are roomy and cut to sit just above the knee, and why the trousers are pleated and wide. The tees follow the same logic, mid-weight and closer to a skate shirt than a golf one.
writeup.4: The landscape part is real, but it operates one level down, in the naming. Every collection ties to a specific stretch of Australian coast and the products take their names from places inside it. Elements is Barnbougle in Tasmania, photographed on the same ground. SOUTH is the Mornington Peninsula. RNP is Royal National Park, south of Sydney. The earliest polos were named after beaches in Sydney Harbour, the one case where they said so outright: “the Clontarf and Nielsen, named after iconic beaches within Sydney Harbour.”
writeup.5: Two other things stand out. They spent seven months sampling fabric before releasing their first polo, landed on a recycled-PET yarn, and wrote about it plainly: “We know we are stepping into an industry which is regarded as one of the biggest polluters on earth. But we don’t plan to follow the footsteps of the past.” In February 2025 they showed at the Paris Golf Gallery during fashion week, their first international outing, in a room shared with Hiroki, Club 72 and Parmore.
writeup.6: The range runs by collection rather than by garment, from the Barnbougle line down to a $4.90 ball marker. Prices come from the American storefront in US dollars, and they ship worldwide.
